articles.title: China launches Shenzhou-24 spacecraft carrying first Pakistani astronaut to its space station, 90 experiments planned
articles.summary: China on Wednesday successfully launched its Shenzhou-24 spacecraft carrying three astronauts, including Pakistani national Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, marking
articles.body: China on Wednesday successfully launched its Shenzhou-24 spacecraft carrying three astronauts, including Pakistani national Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, marking the first time a foreign astronaut has travelled aboard a Chinese mission to its Tiangong space station.The spacecraft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, carrying Ali, 40, alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39. The mission marks the first joint spaceflight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's crewed space programme.Ali, a former Pakistan Air Force pilot, will serve as a payload specialist during the mission. He is expected to conduct scientific experiments and technology tests alongside the Chinese crew before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, according to Chinese state media.Speaking ahead of the launch, Ali described the mission as the beginning of a broader journey in space exploration and cooperation between the two countries.“It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights,” he said in Mandarin.In English, he said the mission “is not a finish line” but a long path, expressing hope that future cooperation would expand from individual astronauts travelling together to multiple joint missions and eventually journeys to the Moon, Mars and beyond.“To every child who’s watching while I’m in orbit: Look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams," he said.More than 90 experiments plannedThe three-member crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during the mission, China's official Xinhua news agency reported.According to state broadcaster CCTV, Ali will undertake four scientific projects covering biotechnology and materials science. One of the experiments will involve photosynthetic microorganisms, including cyanobacteria.Ali's mission will be relatively short, and he is scheduled to return to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, CCTV reported.For Tang, the mission will mark his third visit to the Tiangong space station, making him the first Chinese astronaut to travel there three times. Wu and Ali will be undertaking their first spaceflights.Tang said differences in language, culture and psychology had made preparations for the mission more challenging, but both teams had worked to overcome them.“The labels and operating instructions aboard the spacecraft and space station are all in Chinese, and the Pakistani astronaut began training with virtually no foundation of the language,” he said, adding that he and Wu had also stepped up their English studies.China-Pakistan space cooperationThe mission is part of a space cooperation agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025. It marks a new phase in the two countries' growing partnership in space exploration and technology.Their cooperation has already included Chinese-launched Pakistani satellites, a joint satellite-navigation system and plans for a Pakistani-built lunar rover to fly aboard China's Chang'e mission around 2028.Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif extended his wishes to the astronauts ahead of the launch, describing the mission as a milestone in bilateral relations.“Tomorrow, Pakistan will look to the skies with anticipation, pride and deep gratitude,” he wrote on X.Praising Chinese President Xi Jinping, Sharif said his “visionary leadership and steadfast commitment to Pakistan-China friendship have taken our All-Weather Strategic Cooperative Partnership to unprecedented heights.”He also credited Pakistani scientists, the armed forces and national institutions for their contributions to the country's space programme.“Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas in its journey to outer space,” he said.China targets crewed Moon landing by 2030China's space programme has expanded rapidly as Beijing seeks to strengthen its position in space exploration and compete with the United States.The country is preparing for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030, while NASA is targeting 2028 for its next astronaut landing on the Moon.Since Yuri Gagarin's first human spaceflight in 1961, citizens of around 50 countries have travelled to space. However, only three countries, Russia, the United States and China, have developed the capability to launch their own crewed spacecraft.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Meghan Markle's father Thomas indicted on two counts of possessing child sexual abuse material in US
articles.summary: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Britain's Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, has been indicted on two federal counts of possessing child sexual
articles.body: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Britain's Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, has been indicted on two federal counts of possessing child sexual abuse material in the United States. If convicted, the 82-year-old could face a maximum prison sentence of 40 years.A federal grand jury in Los Angeles returned the indictment on Tuesday, adding a second count to the felony charge initially filed against Markle on November 5, according to Reuters. Each count carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison.Markle was arrested on November 6 at an assisted-living facility in Florida, where he was residing. He is currently in custody in the state and is expected to be transferred to California in the coming weeks to face the charges in a federal court in Los Angeles.According to court filings, investigators found dozens of suspected child sexual abuse images, including photographs, film negatives, slides and books, in two storage units in Los Angeles. An FBI affidavit also alleged that Markle was identified in at least two photographs alongside a naked, prepubescent girl.Some of the material was allegedly linked to the Philippines, where Markle previously lived and had a home. One photograph reportedly showed a naked girl in a room that appeared to be part of a motel chain in the country.Markle has denied the allegations. In an earlier interview with the Daily Mail, he described the claims as "sick lies".Judge rules Markle mentally competent to stand trialThe indictment comes days after a US magistrate judge in Tampa, Florida, ruled that Markle was mentally competent to stand trial following a court-ordered psychiatric evaluation.The assessment found that he understood the proceedings against him and could assist in his own defence, two key requirements for determining whether a defendant is competent to stand trial.According to an Associated Press report citing the psychiatrist's assessment, Markle denied possessing illegal material during his competency interview in mid-November.“Why I am here. What have I done?” the psychiatrist quoted him as saying. “I don’t have any child porn. I have no pictures of naked kids.”The psychiatrist also said Markle was “malingering,” or exaggerating, at times during the assessment.Markle was initially granted bond following his arrest but was detained again days later after allegedly attempting to remove his ankle monitor.Separate investigation in the PhilippinesMarkle is also facing scrutiny in the Philippines, where police have filed criminal complaints against him in Cebu province over alleged violations of laws concerning online sexual abuse and exploitation of children.Philippine police said he was being investigated for possession and intent to distribute illegal child abuse images.The US federal case originated from an investigation initiated last month in the Philippines before authorities examined material allegedly found in storage facilities in Los Angeles.Meghan Markle estranged from fatherThomas Markle has been estranged from his daughter Meghan since the period leading up to her marriage to Prince Harry in 2018.Meghan has previously said she became aware of allegations against her father around that time and was "deeply distressed" by the matter. The estrangement has also meant that her father has had no contact with her two children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Inaction no longer an option': US Army prepares to detonate 4.5 tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa, issues lead dust warnings
articles.summary: The US Army is preparing to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds (4,500 kg) of degraded lead azide at an ammunition plant in Iowa on Wednesday, warning residents
articles.body: The US Army is preparing to detonate nearly 10,000 pounds (4,500 kg) of degraded lead azide at an ammunition plant in Iowa on Wednesday, warning residents about possible exposure to toxic lead dust while assuring them that measures have been put in place to limit its spread.The controlled explosion is scheduled for around 9 am local time (3 pm GMT) at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The Army said the operation was necessary to prevent a potentially dangerous spontaneous explosion as the chemical stockpile continues to deteriorate.“Inaction is no longer an option,” Major General Eric Shirley, who is leading the operation, said.Acting US Army Secretary Adam Telle sought to reassure residents amid concerns about the environmental and health consequences of the blast.“We don’t believe that the public should be in a panic,” Telle said. “Our goal is to keep as much of it as we can here on our Iowa Army Ammunition plant to prevent it from traveling.”The Army said its safety measures include earth barriers around two concrete storage bunkers containing the explosives, misting systems to dampen the surrounding terrain and specialised foam designed to capture particles released during the detonation.Officials also plan to use ballistic gels and thousands of gallons of water to contain the lead dust.Residents warned about possible lead exposureThe Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) issued an alert on Tuesday warning that residents within five miles (8 km) of the blast site may be evacuated.People living between five and 20 miles (8-32 km) from the facility have been advised to remain indoors with windows closed to minimise exposure to airborne particles.The Army released updated maps showing the possible spread of lead dust following the explosion. According to the projections, particles settling on surfaces could travel up to 40 miles from the blast site, extending southwest through southeastern Iowa and into northern Missouri.Airborne particles could travel considerably farther, with projections indicating that they could reach areas nearly 100 miles away within eight hours of the detonation.The Army said it would publish updated dispersal projections every hour, beginning six hours before the scheduled explosion, based on changing weather conditions. A final estimate of the affected area will also be released after the operation.Officials said most of the resulting plume would consist of non-toxic substances, including nitrogen gas, water vapour, sand and soil, while a smaller portion could contain fine lead oxide dust.The US Department of Agriculture estimated that around 350 farms could be affected by the projected plume. It said it would work to ensure that heavy metals and lead do not enter the food chain. Farmers have been advised to move livestock indoors and protect hay bales and water supplies.Why is the Army destroying the chemical stockpile?Lead azide is an explosive chemical used to trigger the detonation of military ammunition. The Army had moved away from using the compound and transferred stockpiles from military installations across the country to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in 2009 for storage and regular monitoring.However, the Army discovered signs of degradation in March that raised concerns about a possible spontaneous explosion.Officials said the material was becoming increasingly volatile and that falling temperatures in the coming days could further increase the risk. The Army initially scheduled the operation for last Friday but postponed it three times to assess safety concerns, improve containment measures and identify favourable weather conditions.The decision to proceed with a controlled detonation followed a court ruling late Monday that allowed the operation to go ahead. The court said the US Environmental Protection Agency had adequately incorporated safeguards to minimise the dispersal of lead dust.Environmental groups had challenged the operation in court, arguing over the potential health and environmental risks. The Army said it had considered alternatives, including chemical neutralisation and thermal treatment, but concluded that controlled detonation was the safest option.“We’ve taken every viable solution and considered it,” Telle said. “In every instance, the answer is controlled detonation is safest.”Health and environmental concernsThe planned explosion has prompted concerns among residents about possible lead contamination, particularly its long-term impact on children, pregnant women, livestock and wildlife.Officials have identified children and pregnant women as groups facing the greatest risk from potential lead exposure.A University of Iowa team is deploying air monitors and collecting soil samples to assess the extent of any contamination following the blast. The monitoring exercise will also examine surfaces where lead particles could accumulate.David Cwiertny, director of the university's Center for Health Effects of Environmental Contamination, said the monitoring would focus on frequently touched surfaces.“The things we are hearing a lot about are playground equipment, furniture, high-touch areas,” he said.Some residents have also expressed concerns about the impact on local water bodies and wildlife.Lucy Giehl, who lives around five miles from the facility, said she was worried about allowing her dogs outside following the explosion.“I don’t know if we’ll be able to swim in the pond or if our dogs can drink out of the pond," she said. “We have bald eagles that fly by out here. There’s so much wildlife, and it’s all in danger.”Iowa leaders seek greater transparencyThe operation has also triggered criticism over the Army's communication with residents and the timing of the detonation, which is scheduled a day before Thanksgiving.Iowa Republican Governor Kim Reynolds said she supported the operation after speaking with military officials. However, Republican Senator Joni Ernst said residents were justified in seeking more information about the potential risks.Iowans “are right to be frustrated” that details about the possibility of lead contamination had not been shared earlier, she said.Ernst said the Army had informed her that the explosion would last “only seconds” and that the dust would dissipate within an hour. Air, soil, surface water and lead residue samples collected before the operation will continue to be monitored afterwards to assess contamination and guide any necessary cleanup.Meanwhile, Telle said the Army was reviewing its weapons storage facilities to prevent similar incidents in the future.For now, he said, the priority was “getting this operation right.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Flights delayed at Chicago O’Hare airport as ground radar system suffers outage
articles.summary: Flights bound for Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport were briefly grounded on Tuesday after an outage of the airport’s ground radar system.
articles.body: Flights bound for Chicago’s O’Hare International Airport were briefly grounded on Tuesday after an outage of the airport’s ground radar system. The disruption to traffic came during the Thanksgiving holiday rush, delaying many passengers.The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted the ground stop after a short while, transitioning to a ground delay programme before cancelling it later in the day. Flights are still facing delays, with the FAA warning that another ground stop could be imposed if congestion builds up on runways and taxiways.The outage was believed to be linked to the ASD-X ground surveillance radar system, which tracks aircraft and vehicles on airport runways and taxiways to help prevent collisions.The FAA said technicians were working to repair the equipment. At one point, delays for flights headed to O’Hare were averaging 47 minutes, while the airport’s arrival capacity had been reduced to 72 flights an hour from its usual 100.About 350 flights, or 12% of traffic, had been delayed earlier in the day, with most of the affected flights bound for Chicago. Flight-tracking site FlightAware later reported around 400 delayed arrivals and departures, including delays caused by other factors.The FAA also warned of a shortage of air traffic controllers at Chicago’s Terminal Radar Approach Control centre from 8.30 pm, which could further affect traffic in the region.Tuesday’s disruption marked the second ground stop at O’Hare this week. Flights were halted on Monday because of staffing issues at the Chicago TRACON.Nearly 1.67 million passengers are expected to pass through O’Hare over the seven-day Thanksgiving travel period, up 7.2% from 2025.You use AI every day. articles.title: What billionaires paid nearly $400 million to stop in California has existed in Norway since 1892
articles.summary: Earlier this month, a group of billionaires, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, collaborated and spent $378 million to defeat Prop 40 – a one-time
articles.body: Earlier this month, a group of billionaires, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, collaborated and spent $378 million to defeat Prop 40 – a one-time tax on billionaires. But Norway introduced a wealth tax back in 1892 – when the US was deep in the Gilded Age, an era when industrialists like John D. Rockefeller and Andrew Carnegie amassed unprecedented fortunes amid stark economic inequality. Now more than 130 years later, the country still collects that tax even as the US is once again grappling with extreme wealth concentration that by some measures surpasses Gilded Age levels, Fortune reported. While both countries debate taxing net worth, they are working from fundamentally different blueprints, a gap that shapes how much money a wealth tax raises, who leaves the country, and whether it can survive legal challenges.Norway’s model: broad, low and modestUnlike US proposals aimed squarely at billionaires, Norway’s wealth tax applies to a wide swath of the population, including middle-class homeowners and savers with substantial assets and low debt.As per 2026 tax rates, net wealth above NOK 1.9 million (roughly $197,000) is taxed at a combined local and national rate of 1%, with the threshold doubled for married couples. Above NOK 21.5 million (about $2.2 million), the rate edges up to 1.1%. According to Tax Foundation economist Cristina Enache, the levy generated roughly 0.6% of Norway’s GDP and 1.5% of total tax revenue in 2024 – a relatively small share that leads economists to caution against assuming a US version would produce massive windfalls.Although total revenue from the tax has continued to climb despite an exodus of millionaires, a poll ahead of Norway’s September 2025 election showed 39% of Norwegians favored keeping or raising it, 23% wanted it reduced, and 28% wanted it abolished. Economists also note that Norway’s massive sovereign wealth fund – the largest in the world – is built primarily on petroleum taxes, licensing fees, and state ownership interests rather than wealth-tax receipts.US proposals target fewer than 1,000 people at steep ratesIn contrast, leading American proposals focused narrowly on ultra-high-net-worth individuals at a much higher rate. The Make Billionaires Pay Their Fair Share Act, introduced by Sanders and Khanna in March, would levy a 5% annual tax on Americans worth more than $1 billion – a group of 938 people by the sponsors' count.Projected revenue from a 5% federal billionaire tax varies sharply depending on assumptions around tax avoidance. Sanders and Khanna cite estimates from economists Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman projecting $4.4 trillion over a decade to fund $3,000 direct payments to households earning $150,000 or less, alongside housing, health care, and childcare programs.Assuming higher rates of avoidance and factoring in compliance costs, the Tax Foundation estimates a 5% tax above $1 billion would bring in roughly $1.5 trillion over 10 years, or about $3.3 trillion under alternative assumptions applied to the Sanders-Khanna bill.A constitutional hurdle Norway never facedBeyond enforcement and valuation headaches, a federal wealth tax in the US faces a constitutional barrier that does not exist in Norway. While states are permitted to tax wealth, the US Constitution requires “direct” federal taxes to be apportioned among the states by population, with the 16th Amendment carving out an exception only for taxes on income.Legal watchers closely followed the 2024 Supreme Court ruling in Moore v. United States, which involved a dispute over unrealized income. Although the court ruled on narrow grounds without deciding the constitutionality of a wealth tax, four justices – just one short of a majority – signaled that income must be realised before it can be taxed.Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Two arrested after masked men break into Prince William and Kate Middleton's country home
articles.summary: Two men have been arrested on suspicion for breaking into Prince William and Kate Middleton’s country home, Anmer Hall, in Norfolk on Monday.
articles.body: Two men have been arrested on suspicion for breaking into Prince William and Kate Middleton’s country home, Anmer Hall, in Norfolk on Monday.The men were arrested on suspicion of burglary and trespass, according to The Times. Police said the estate was unoccupied at the time of the break-in. The suspects remain in custody.Anmer Hall, a 10-bedroom Georgian house on the Sandringham Estate, is used by the Prince and Princess of Wales as a country retreat. The couple often spend weekends and holidays there with their three children, Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis.The property also holds personal significance for Catherine, who recuperated there following surgery and cancer treatment in 2024.The house was built in 1802 and became part of the Sandringham Estate in 1896, when it was purchased by the future King Edward VII. It was later leased to several members of the British aristocracy, including the Duke and Duchess of Kent.William and Kate’s move to Anmer Hall was confirmed in 2013, following their marriage and the birth of Prince George. The couple moved in two years later after a major renovation, which reportedly cost around $2 million and included improvements to the house and measures to increase privacy.The property has since served as a family retreat, including during the Covid-19 lockdown. The Prince and Princess of Wales now spend most of their time at Forest Lodge in Windsor, while continuing to use Anmer Hall as a country escape.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Delhi SIR: Last day to file claims, objections on Wednesday; final roll on December 22
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Wednesday will be the last day for filing claims and objections under the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of Delhi's electoral roll.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Wednesday will be the last day for filing claims and objections under the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of Delhi's electoral roll. The final roll will be published on Dec 22.The office of the chief electoral officer (CEO) Tuesday said Delhi had received 3.3 lakh applications seeking inclusion of names in the voter list since Aug 31 when the SIR draft electoral roll was published and nearly 47.6 lakh voters were left out of around 1.45 crore listed in the last roll. It contained around 97.5 lakh names. SIR began in Delhi on June 30.The CEO office said 3.3 lakh Form 6 applications were received between Aug 31 and Nov 23. Form 6 is used for inclusion of names in the electoral rolls. The office also received 35,155 Form 7 applications seeking deletion of names and 1.2 lakh Form 8 applications for corrections in voter details, shifting of residence or replacement of EPIC cards. Another 610 Form 6A applications came from overseas electors seeking registration."No further extension of the claims and objections period was likely as the electoral roll revision process has to be completed within the revised schedule," said an official. The original deadline of Oct 30 was extended last month till Nov 25 to allow additional time to the deleted as well as first-time voters.Among districts, West recorded the highest number of Form 6 applications at 39,792, followed by North East (32,341), North West (31,375), East (31,359) and South East (31,518). New Delhi recorded the lowest number at 5,741.South East district received the highest number of Form 7 applications at 4,808, followed by South (4,719), North East (4,305) and West (3,614). For Form 8, North East topped the list with 16,729 applications, followed by West (12,999), East (12,718) and South West (11,927).The deadline extension pushed back the subsequent stages of the revision. The deadline for disposal of claims and objections was pushed from Nov 30 to Dec 15, while publication of the final electoral roll was rescheduled from Dec 4 to 22.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: China link in CIA data breach? How hackers used AI tool to expose unclassified information - report
articles.summary: A cyberattack targeting an intelligence analysis system used by the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and at least two other American intelligence
articles.body: A cyberattack targeting an intelligence analysis system used by the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) and at least two other American intelligence agencies may have involved an artificial intelligence hacking tool linked to China, according to a report by The New York Times. The breach exposed some unclassified information, although officials said classified material was not compromised.The intrusion affected an open-source intelligence system used by the CIA, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA) and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI), people familiar with the matter told the newspaper.Investigators have not identified those responsible for the breach. However, initial indications, including the alleged use of an AI-powered hacking tool called Artex, have raised suspicions of possible Chinese involvement, according to two people familiar with the investigation.The incident was reportedly resolved, and officials said there had been no disruption to critical capabilities. The exact nature and volume of information accessed by the hackers remain unclear.What is the AI hacking tool Artex?According to people familiar with the investigation, the hackers are believed to have used Artex, an AI-powered cybersecurity tool released earlier this year by a Chinese engineer.The tool was initially developed to help organisations identify cybersecurity vulnerabilities and strengthen their digital defences. However, it was made publicly available in July and has since allegedly been adapted by malicious actors to carry out cyberattacks.Cybersecurity researchers have linked Artex to dozens of attacks targeting businesses worldwide, including organisations in Japan and South Korea, according to the report.Although investigators suspect a possible Chinese connection, they have not established who carried out the attack or whether it was directed by the Chinese government.China's intelligence agencies and their network of contractors have previously been accused by Western officials of targeting US government agencies and private companies through cyberattacks. Beijing has routinely denied such allegations.What information was exposed in the breach?The compromised system was used by American intelligence agencies to analyse open-source information and generate intelligence assessments.Open-source intelligence, commonly known as OSINT, involves collecting and analysing publicly available and commercially sourced information. This can include social media posts, satellite imagery, online databases and information purchased from commercial data vendors.Although much of this information is publicly accessible, combining different datasets can reveal sensitive details and provide intelligence agencies with insights that may not be apparent from individual sources.The system is used by intelligence agencies to analyse such information alongside other intelligence sources to support their assessments.According to people familiar with the incident, the breach exposed unclassified information, while classified material remained secure. The authorities have not disclosed precisely what information was accessed.An official from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence said there had been no disruption to critical capabilities. The CIA declined to comment, while the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency did not respond to a request for comment, the report said.US intelligence agencies face multiple cyber incidentsThe latest breach comes amid heightened concerns over cybersecurity vulnerabilities across American government institutions, following a series of reported intrusions and technical disruptions.The National Security Agency's (NSA) internal classified communications network experienced a prolonged outage between November 17 and November 20. The disruption was subsequently resolved, although officials and businesses said it was not caused by a cyberattack.Separately, US President Donald Trump appeared to confirm last week that the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a nationwide database used by local, state and federal law enforcement agencies to exchange information about criminal suspects, had been hacked.The FBI is investigating the incident, according to people familiar with the matter.The US Department of Agriculture also discovered a cybersecurity incident last week that forced some of its internal applications to be taken offline, according to a department employee. The incident was earlier reported by Nextgov.These developments have intensified scrutiny of the security of government networks and critical information systems.US intelligence chief seeks to reassure publicAmid growing concerns over the incidents, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton sought to reassure the public about the cybersecurity situation during television appearances on Sunday.Clayton, whom Trump recently appointed as acting cyber director, addressed concerns surrounding recent technological disruptions, including the nationwide flight grounding earlier this month. Officials have attributed that incident to problems associated with router maintenance rather than a cyberattack.Responding to questions about the reported breach of the FBI's crime database, Clayton said such incidents were not uncommon and that authorities were handling the matter.“Cyberprobing, cyberincidents, they have been part of the American economy, part of the American life for a long time,” Clayton said on ABC's 'This Week'.“And what we’re hearing about the FBI, and what I’ve talked to them about is, they have an incident. They’re dealing with it in the ordinary course.”The latest intelligence agency breach adds to concerns over the vulnerability of US government networks, particularly as artificial intelligence tools are increasingly being used to identify software weaknesses and potentially exploit them.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ohio man spent nearly 20 years building a rock-filled sanctuary for troubled young people, with winding paths, a barrel-shaped cottage and a memorial to the state's war dead
articles.summary: The Temple of Tolerance, a rock-filled garden sanctuary in Ohio created by Jim Bowsher, was designed as a refuge where troubled young people could feel
articles.body: The Temple of Tolerance, a rock-filled garden sanctuary in Ohio created by Jim Bowsher, was designed as a refuge where troubled young people could feel accepted. Winding pathways circle the central temple and lead visitors past a barrel-shaped cottage, quiet alcoves for rest and a memorial to the state's war dead. Bowsher regards the project as his undoubted master work, and it grew from a conviction about human nature that the site was built to express. Anyone can walk the grounds, which were built slowly, stone by stone, for people whose family lives or close relationships had left them hurt.A refuge for young people hurt by troubled family lives took nearly two decades of rock movingAccording to Jim Bowsher's website, the Temple of Tolerance was developed as a refuge for young people battered by dysfunctional family dynamics or other destructive relationships. Bowsher spent nearly two decades moving and precisely placing innumerable rocks, many of them massive, and added other ornamental features to complete the grounds.A door from a cell that once held Dillinger gang members is hidden along the winding pathsThe meandering pathways around the central temple conceal countless surprises. Among them is a door from a jail cell that once held members of the Dillinger gang, set along the route alongside spaces made for meditation.Bowsher has described the temple on his website as "more a state of mind than a place", the physical form of a philosophical idea. The role it plays in the surrounding community reflects his guiding belief that all people are born with a natural capacity for goodness.The temple and its war memorial stay open year-round, and visitors reach them by the side drivewayThe website points to the many adults who credit the temple and Bowsher's friendship with guiding them through difficult childhood and teenage years as a testament to that belief.The Temple of Tolerance and the Memorial to Ohio War Dead are open throughout the year and free to the public, the site says. Visitors enter by the driveway to the right of the house. A donation box on the porch collects contributions toward maintaining both works.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Bengaluru woman’s Rs 12.7 lakh Groww portfolio falls to Rs 84,508 after tech glitch during Rs 10 lakh withdrawal; firm told to refund Rs 11.85 lakh with 6% interest and pay Rs 12,000
articles.summary: BENGALURU: Imagine watching your savings grow to over Rs 12 lakh on an investment app, only to see the balance shrink to under Rs 1 lakh the moment you
articles.body: BENGALURU: Imagine watching your savings grow to over Rs 12 lakh on an investment app, only to see the balance shrink to under Rs 1 lakh the moment you try to withdraw your own money. That is what a city woman faced when the Groww app displayed a sudden, unexplained error after she sought a redemption. The Bengaluru (Urban) District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has held the platform liable for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.The saga began when Ranjana Priya, a resident of HSR Layout, Sector 2, trusted the platform's market reputation and assurances and invested a total of Rs 8.12 lakhs through systematic investment plans (SIPs) on the Groww app. Favourable market performance pushed her portfolio up significantly, and the official dashboard showed its valuation had reached Rs 12,70,404 as of November 26, 2025.Citing urgent personal and financial requirements, she placed a digital request for a partial redemption of Rs 10 lakh. What followed, she said, were "alarming errors". The dashboard updated to show her total invested amount as just Rs 84,508, wiping out the rest of her portfolio value.Priya said she ran from pillar to post, raising support tickets by phone and email and complaining to SEBI on November 27. Nothing was resolved. On November 30, Groww credited a mere Rs 15,500 to her bank account. By her reconciliation, her total investment value stood at Rs 12.70 lakhs. After accounting for the amount redeemed, Rs 11.85 lakhs was left unaccounted for.She then raised statutory grievances on the e-Jagriti platform through WhatsApp four times between December 7 and December 25, 2025. The opposite parties neither corrected their financial records nor refunded the balance. Leaving her with no option, Priya approached the commission on April 22, 2026, and sought a refund for mental agony, harassment and financial hardship.She named Groww Invest Tech Pvt Ltd and Nextbillion Technology Pvt Ltd (Groww)/Billionbrains Garage Ventures Pvt Ltd. Both appeared through counsel but did not file their written version within the statutory 45 days. Their version was taken as not filed, in line with a judgment of the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, and despite sufficient opportunities, they never mounted a defence.After going through the records and hearing arguments, the commission observed that her allegations stood unchallenged as the firms had forfeited their right to defence. It accepted as true her digital records, including the portfolio value of Rs 12.7 lakhs and the redemption request for Rs 10 lakh. The platform's act of reducing the visible portfolio value to Rs 84,508, coupled with its complete failure to respond to four separate institutional warnings from the National Grievance Helpline, amounted to deficiency in service and unfair trade practice, it said. It termed the withholding of Rs 11.85 lakhs belonging to a retail investor "completely unauthorised, illegal and high handed".The commission added that a digital investment platform cannot hold a consumer's hard-earned savings hostage under the guise of an unrectified technical glitch or internal database error. The documents showed beyond doubt that of her Rs 12. 7 lakhs portfolio, Rs 11.85 lakhs remained unaccounted for and was withheld without valid legal justification, causing mental agony and financial distress to a complainant dependent on her savings.The commission, comprising president Ramachandra MS and members Nandini H Kumbhar and Savitha Airani directed both firms, jointly and severally, to refund Rs 11,85,896 with 6% annual interest from the date of redemption until actual realisation. articles.title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan seeks execution delay, says he was defending Taliban
articles.summary: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan has asked a federal court to delay his scheduled execution, saying he intends to argue that he was defending the Taliban
articles.body: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan has asked a federal court to delay his scheduled execution, saying he intends to argue that he was defending the Taliban from an unlawful US military attack.In a court filing signed by Hasan on Tuesday, he said he intended to demonstrate that the military court’s judgment and his death sentence had been obtained and were being maintained in violation of his federal constitutional and statutory rights.The filing could delay the Trump administration’s plans to execute Hasan on December 3. A hearing has been scheduled for Wednesday morning.Hasan, who is representing himself with assistance from lawyers at the American Civil Liberties Union’s Capital Punishment Project, said he intended to continue representing himself in the legal fight.Hasan wants to revive defence barred at trialOne of Hasan’s central arguments is that he was prevented from presenting a defence that his actions were legally justified because he was trying to protect the Afghan Taliban from what he described as an unlawful attack by the US Army.Hasan had argued that he was acting in “defense of others”, according to court documents. However, the military judge barred him from presenting that argument during his 2013 trial.After dismissing his lawyers and choosing to represent himself, Hasan largely remained silent during the three-week trial. While the military called nearly 90 witnesses, Hasan called none in his defence and made no closing argument.A military jury found him guilty of multiple counts of murder and attempted murder for the shooting, which left 13 people dead and 32 wounded.The case has been assigned to US district judge Tony Mattivi in Kansas, where Hasan is being held at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth. Mattivi was nominated by president Donald Trump and confirmed by the Senate in June.What happened in the Fort Hood attack?On November 5, 2009, Hasan walked into the Soldier Readiness Processing Center at Fort Hood, Texas, where soldiers were waiting for medical tests and preparing for deployment.He opened fire with a handgun fitted with laser sights, killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others.Hasan was shot by law enforcement officers during the attack, leaving him paralysed from the waist down and confined to a wheelchair.He was convicted by a military jury in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. The jury sentenced him to death.Execution controversy and survivors’ objectionsTrump authorised Hasan’s execution on the recommendation of defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The execution, scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, would be the first US military execution by firing squad since World War II and the first military execution since 1961.The plan drew controversy after Hegseth announced that the execution would be public and the Pentagon confirmed it would be livestreamed. Critics from both parties raised concerns that broadcasting the execution could fuel radicalisation and turn it into a spectacle.Trump later said the execution would not be livestreamed, but that immediate family members of the victims could witness it in person if they chose.The latest court filing comes amid further dispute over who will be allowed to attend. Military officials have denied requests from three survivors of the 2009 shooting to witness the execution, citing regulations, security and space constraints.The survivors argued that the military should recognise them as victims under a broader definition that includes direct physical, emotional or financial harm. The Army rejected their appeal, saying regulations specify who may attend a military execution.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Seattle man hid $39,600 inherited from his father during bankruptcy; court revokes his discharge of nearly $4 million in debt after finding fraud
articles.summary: A Seattle man lost more than $3.9 million in bankruptcy discharge after a court found that he had concealed inheritance rights and an interest in a
articles.body: A Seattle man lost more than $3.9 million in bankruptcy discharge after a court found that he had concealed inheritance rights and an interest in a business. The Bankruptcy Court for the Western District of Washington entered judgment revoking Nevin Middleton’s Chapter 7 discharge on October 20. As a result, Middleton remains liable for his debts, and creditors may pursue payment from him after the case is closed.According to the US Department of Justice, he had received about $39,600 from his father’s probate estate but failed to disclose the inheritance and business interest in his bankruptcy filings. The ruling followed a trial victory by the Justice Department’s US Trustee Program (USTP), which had sought to revoke the discharge over those undisclosed funds.Middleton’s failed construction business led him to seek bankruptcy reliefMiddleton first filed an individual Chapter 11 reorganisation case to address debts arising from a failed custom home construction business. The case was later converted to a Chapter 7 liquidation. In April 2024, he received a Chapter 7 discharge covering $3,967,997 in unsecured debt. Most of that amount involved claims brought by creditors who had invested in his projects.The discharge had been granted in April 2024. The court’s later decision revoked that relief after finding that Middleton had obtained it through fraud. The ruling means the debts were no longer discharged, and creditors are free to seek payment from him once the bankruptcy case is closed.Middleton disclosed his $39,600 inheritance months after receiving debt reliefSeveral months after receiving the discharge, Middleton appeared at an evidentiary hearing concerning his claim to a homestead exemption on some of his real estate. During that hearing, he disclosed for the first time that he had received two deposits from his late father’s probate estate. The distributions totalled about $39,600 and had been paid after he filed for bankruptcy but before he received the discharge.The money went into a business bank account that Middleton controlled. However, his original bankruptcy schedules and statements did not list his inheritance rights or his interest in the business connected to the account. The disclosure came only months after the discharge was granted.US Trustee Program took Middleton to trial over undisclosed inheritanceThe US Trustee Program’s Seattle office investigated the undisclosed funds. Investigators found that Middleton had instructed his sister, who was the executor of their father’s probate estate, to send the distributions to a business account. The private trustee administering Middleton’s bankruptcy case did not know of that business account.At trial on the US Trustee Program’s complaint seeking revocation of the discharge, Middleton gave a different explanation for the money. He testified that the payments were loans from his sister. The bankruptcy court considered the evidence before reaching its decision. It concluded that Middleton had knowingly and fraudulently failed to report the funds to the Chapter 7 trustee. The court also found that he had obtained his discharge by fraud.Court ruling leaves Middleton responsible for his debtsThe Bankruptcy Court for the Western District of Washington entered judgment on October 20, revoking Middleton’s Chapter 7 bankruptcy discharge.With the discharge revoked, Middleton remains liable for his debts. Creditors are free to pursue payment from him after the bankruptcy case is closed. USTP Director Stephen V. Falanga said, “The bankruptcy discharge is the key to a fresh start, but debtors must be transparent about their financial affairs to receive it. The USTP remains steadfast in its commitment to protect the integrity of the bankruptcy system from dishonest debtors.”Disclaimer: This article is based on the US Department of Justice’s announcement regarding the Bankruptcy Court for the Western District of Washington’s judgment revoking Nevin Middleton’s Chapter 7 bankruptcy discharge. The Times of India has not independently verified the details of the bankruptcy proceedings or the findings reported by the court.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: South Carolina homeowner says 2 proposed highway routes could run through her home as $1.56 billion highway project threatens to wipe out her son's house
articles.summary: A proposed $1.56 billion highway extension in South Carolina has left a homeowner worried about the future of her family after two possible routes were
articles.body: A proposed $1.56 billion highway extension in South Carolina has left a homeowner worried about the future of her family after two possible routes were found to pass through her house. Jenny Cooper, who lives in Juniper Bay outside Conway, said the proposed alignments could force her family off their property, with one of the routes potentially wiping out her son's house as well. The project, intended to improve traffic movement and connectivity across Horry County, has triggered concerns among residents over potential displacement, property loss and environmental damage. Cooper said she understands why a new highway is needed but fears that rising property prices could make it difficult for her family to find another place where they can continue living together.Two proposed highway routes could pass through South Carolina homeowner's houseCooper raised her concerns during a public meeting at the Horry County Government and Justice Center, where residents gathered to discuss plans for the SC-22 highway extension.According to WPDE, she said two of the proposed routes could pass directly through her home in Juniper Bay. The possible alignments have raised questions about what would happen to families whose houses and land fall within the proposed corridors.Cooper is particularly concerned about the impact on her son's property. She explained that one possible route could cut through their land, potentially leaving her son's house directly in the path of the proposed highway."Where this land is or this road's coming through, it's going to cut our land in half. So, my son's house will be completely took out if it goes that direction," Cooper said.She also expressed concern about finding another property where she, her son and his family could continue living together, particularly as land prices continue to rise.What is the $1.56 billion South Carolina highway project?The proposed development is an extension of South Carolina Highway 22, also known as SC-22. Previously referred to as the Southern Evacuation Lifeline, the project is intended to improve transportation connections in Horry County and surrounding areas.The approximately 28-mile extension is planned to connect US Highway 501 near Conway with US Highway 17 in the Murrells Inlet area, close to the Horry-Georgetown county line.Officials have described the project as a way to reduce traffic congestion, improve access to essential services and provide another connection across the Waccamaw River. Hurricane evacuation has also been cited as one of the potential benefits.The estimated cost of the wider project is approximately $1.56 billion, including construction and environmental mitigation. However, the project remains in the planning and environmental review stages.Three possible routes remain under considerationThe highway extension has undergone several rounds of route assessments. Officials initially examined 22 potential alignments before narrowing the options through subsequent screening.Three alternatives, identified as Routes 2, 3 and 4, remain under consideration.The proposed alignments cover different parts of Horry County:Alternative 2: Covers the Juniper Bay and Singleton Crossroads areas.Alternative 3: Passes through the Timberlake area.Alternative 4: Covers the Guiton Crossing area and passes near St. James High School.The alternatives have generated concerns among residents who fear losing their homes, farmland and other parts of their properties if a particular alignment is selected.Residents of The Farm at Timberlake have also raised concerns about Alternative 3, which could potentially affect dozens of homes in the neighbourhood.Environmental concerns surrounding the proposed highwayThe highway proposal has also attracted opposition from environmental campaigners concerned about its potential impact on the Waccamaw River region and nearby protected habitats.One of the major concerns involves the Waccamaw National Wildlife Refuge, which protects wetlands, bottomland hardwood forests and habitats used by numerous wildlife species.Environmental advocates have warned that highway construction could disturb natural habitats, affect wetlands and waterways, and fragment wildlife corridors. They have also raised concerns about potential effects on water quality and flood-prone areas.The US Army Corps of Engineers is overseeing the federal environmental review process, which will examine the potential consequences of the proposed alternatives.Residents and environmental organisations have argued that the project's impact on surrounding communities and ecosystems should be carefully considered before officials select a route.Environmental campaigners question highway's evacuation purposeThe project's earlier name, Southern Evacuation Lifeline, has also become a point of disagreement between officials and environmental advocates.State and county officials have described the highway as potentially useful during hurricane evacuations. However, Amy Armstrong, who leads the South Carolina Environmental Law Project, questioned whether the proposed road would effectively serve that purpose.According to WPDE, Armstrong said the Army Corps of Engineers had previously rejected the project's description as an evacuation route.She argued that the highway would eventually connect with US Highway 501, where motorists could encounter significant traffic congestion.The Corps has identified reducing traffic congestion and improving access to services on both sides of the Waccamaw River as key objectives of the project.Officials say no final route has been selectedHorry County officials have stressed that the proposed alignments are still being evaluated and that no final decision has been made.Thomas Bell, the county's public information director, acknowledged that homeowners could become concerned when they see maps showing potential highway routes passing through their properties.He said the maps were being presented to inform residents and gather their feedback rather than indicate that a particular route had been approved.The Army Corps of Engineers is also considering public comments as part of its environmental review. Residents have been encouraged to share concerns about property impacts, environmental consequences and other aspects of the proposal.The Corps is expected to prepare a Draft Environmental Impact Statement as the review progresses, followed by another opportunity for public feedback.The project is currently projected to move towards construction around 2030, with completion targeted around 2035.You use AI every day. articles.title: Amazon took out a notice in a newspaper of a small village in the US, and made a request for public hearing; meeting happened with the town, telling the company: Not interested
articles.summary: Amazon’s plan to launch a drone delivery hub in a small Massachusetts town became public through a legal notice in a local weekly newspaper.
articles.body: ​Amazon’s plan to launch a drone delivery hub in a small Massachusetts town became public through a legal notice in a local weekly newspaper. The company took its proposal to a public hearing in Westborough, then faced more than 200 people at a separate community meeting. Residents pressed Amazon on noise, safety and privacy. Weeks later, the town sent a clearer ‘not interested’ message, voting to restrict commercial drone operations. Amazon then withdrew its application.​For Westborough resident Christine Farmer, it began with a notice she almost missed. She usually skipped the legal notices in the Community Advocate, but this one caught her eye. The proposed launch site was less than two miles from her home. Farmer knew the appeal of fast delivery. She had once nearly hugged an Amazon driver who brought her a package she needed that same day. At the September 15 public hearing, though, she pulled out her phone to work out what hundreds of drone deliveries might mean for her neighbourhood. At 600 deliveries over 12 hours, she calculated, there would be almost one a minute.​Amazon told the Westborough Planning Board that its Prime Air drones could deliver packages weighing up to five pounds in 30 minutes or less. The service would reach customers within 7.5 miles of the company’s warehouse at 64 Otis Street, with drones dropping parcels into yards or driveways from about 13 feet above the ground.​What Westborough residents told Amazon​Eight days after the public hearing, Amazon held a separate community meeting at a local hotel. More than 200 people turned up, including residents of neighbouring towns, according to The New York Times. They asked what the drones would sound like, how often they would fly and what the service could mean for privacy, safety and property values.​Tareq Wafaie, an Amazon economic development manager, said the company expected to start with about six drones. He told the audience that customers wanted faster deliveries and pointed to parents who might need diapers while at home with a sick child. No one in the room spoke in favour of the proposal, NYT reported.​By then, Westborough’s building commissioner had already determined that the drone hub qualified as an accessory use of the existing warehouse. Farmer and fellow resident Rod Jané argued that a new operation of that kind should require a special permit. They drafted an appeal overnight, gathered 25 signatures and filed it on September 25, just before the deadline.​Last month, Westborough residents packed the high school auditorium for a special town meeting. They voted 510–13 to adopt a bylaw restricting where commercial drones could take off, land and drop off packages. The measure requires state review and approval before it can take effect.​Eleven days later, Amazon asked to withdraw its application. The Planning Board accepted the request earlier this month. The withdrawal leaves Amazon free to submit a revised plan.Fearless legend or grounded realist? Rate yourself on 11 categories in the Great Indian Confidence Survey – find out in 3–6 min

articles.title: Five years after a nine-year-old boy died of brain cancer, his family fulfilled his wish by opening a 15,000-square-foot children's museum inside a hospital to give young patients a place to play
articles.summary: Some people, even after they are gone, leave such a profound mark on the world that their presence continues to be felt in the lives of people they never
articles.body: Some people, even after they are gone, leave such a profound mark on the world that their presence continues to be felt in the lives of people they never got to meet. For the Beery family, that legacy belongs to their nine-year-old son, Walker. Five years after losing him to brain cancer, his parents have fulfilled a wish he once made during his hospital stays: to give other children like him somewhere to play, explore and, even for a little while, forget that they are sick.On November 17, 2026, Manning Family Children's in New Orleans, Louisiana, celebrated the opening of Walker's Imaginarium, a 15,000-square-foot children's museum built within the hospital. It is believed to be the first museum of its kind to be incorporated into a children's hospital, transforming an idea that began with a little boy's longing for a happier hospital experience into a space that can now bring joy to thousands of young patients and their families.Why Walker dreamt of a ImaginariumAs reported by PEOPLE, Walker was just 7 years old when he was diagnosed with medulloblastoma, a rare and aggressive form of brain cancer, in August 2019. What followed was a difficult 2 year journey involving surgeries, lengthy hospital stays, chemotherapy and radiation. Yet, in the middle of everything he was going through, Walker was thinking about something beyond his own illness.During his time in hospital, he often wished there was somewhere he could go outside his room, get some fresh air and take a break from the endless cycle of treatments. His initial idea was a butterfly garden where children receiving care could spend time outdoors and enjoy a little distraction. It was a simple wish, but one that said a great deal about the little boy behind it. Even while dealing with an experience no child should have to endure, he wanted other children to have something to look forward to.Walker passed away in September 2021, aged 9. But his idea did not leave with him.In the years that followed, his parents, Taylor and Angel Beery, worked to turn his wish into something much bigger. Together with the nonprofit organisation Kids Join The Fight, which Walker helped establish, they began working towards creating a space where children receiving hospital care could experience the kind of joy that often gets pushed aside by illness.The result is a two-storey museum that feels a world away from the clinical surroundings of a hospital. And rather fittingly for a project born in New Orleans, the city itself has been woven into almost every corner of it.Inside the ImaginariumAccording to Good News Network, children entering the museum are welcomed by interactive lights, marching band music and percussion instruments arranged around a whimsical tree. There is even a year-round Mardi Gras parade, complete with a special float called the Krewe of Walker. An enormous LED butterfly hangs overhead, its wings moving in response to children playing on an accessible swing below it.Elsewhere, young visitors can explore an imaginative bayou, enjoy airboat rides, wander through a colourful forest or take part in a miniature sports field. There is also a lemonade stand and a playful recreation of Louisiana's famous front-porch culture, complete with a crawfish boil. For children who fancy something a little more competitive, an outdoor terrace houses a nine-hole miniature golf course inspired by local landmarks, including an oversized alligator and a fireworks display at the Superdome.But the museum is not just about running around and having fun. Its design takes into account that every child has different needs, particularly those who are undergoing treatment or have limited mobility. According to Manning Family Children's, the space includes wheelchair-accessible activities, sensory experiences and quieter areas where children and their families can simply sit together. The idea is to make play accessible to everyone, regardless of their physical or medical circumstances.There is also a dedicated classroom planned for the second floor, which will support children who miss out on school because of prolonged hospital stays. An interactive multimedia studio, developed in partnership with the Ryan Seacrest Foundation, is expected to open in February 2027.How the family brought the idea to lifeSpeaking to PEOPLE, Walker's father, Taylor, said the family was proud that the promise they had made had finally been delivered. Recalling his son's approach to his illness, he shared that Walker never pretended things were easy. He simply refused to let the pain become the only thing that defined his experience.That thought seems to sit at the very heart of the project. As Lucio Fragoso, president and CEO of Manning Family Children's, explained in the hospital's announcement, while it may not always be possible to change why a child is admitted to hospital, it is possible to change what being there feels like.The project, which took five years of planning and construction, has been funded entirely through philanthropic contributions, with patient families, medical teams, architects and designers helping bring the idea to life. As reported by Becker's Hospital Review, Manning Family Children's has also become the first hospital to join the Association of Children's Museums, making the initiative an important step towards bringing the experience of a children's museum into healthcare settings.Contribution beyond the museumThe family has also continued Walker's work beyond the museum. Through Kids Join The Fight, they support paediatric brain cancer research and provide financial assistance to families navigating childhood cancer. The organisation was founded to ensure that other children and their families have access to the support and resources they need during an incredibly difficult time.It is difficult to imagine a more beautiful way to honour a child's memory. What began as a little boy wishing for somewhere to escape his hospital room has become a 15,000-square-foot space where other children can make music, play games, discover new things and spend time with the people they love. The museum cannot undo what happened to Walker, nor can it make the experience of childhood illness any less difficult for the families who walk through its doors. But it can give them something that hospital corridors often leave little room for: ordinary childhood moments. And somewhere in between all those giggles and chatters, a 9-year old boy looks over smiling, seeing his Imaginarium exactly as he imagined.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: An Arizona woman lived with her partner in the same Phoenix house for 24 years, but he never divorced his estranged wife; after his death, an appeals court upheld the legal wife's ownership of the home
articles.summary: An Arizona woman who spent 24 years living in a Phoenix house with her partner has failed to secure ownership of the property after his death.
articles.body: An Arizona woman who spent 24 years living in a Phoenix house with her partner has failed to secure ownership of the property after his death. An appeals court has ruled in favour of his estranged wife, who had left the house nearly 25 years earlier but was still legally married to him.According to the judgement, the dispute centred on a house bought by Troy Torrence and Rita Mack in 1998. The couple purchased the Phoenix property together, with an arrangement that allowed the surviving owner to inherit the other's share.Their relationship broke down the following year, and Mack moved out. However, the couple never legally ended their marriage or changed the ownership arrangement for the house.In 2000, Dimica Hicks moved into the property with Torrence. She continued to live there until his death in September 2024. After his death, Hicks was appointed to handle his estate and approached the court seeking rights over the house.Hicks argued that her long stay at the property and financial contributions towards it gave her a claim to ownership. She also sought repayment for expenses related to the house. However, a lower court rejected her ownership claim and later refused her demand for compensation.The Arizona Court of Appeals has now upheld that decision. In a ruling filed on Monday, the court said Mack became the sole owner after Torrence's death because their joint ownership agreement remained in place.Why the 24-year stay did not give her ownershipHicks argued that she had lived in the house long enough to claim it through adverse possession, a legal route through which someone may acquire rights over property occupied for a specified period under certain conditions.But the court found that the circumstances of her stay did not support such a claim. Hicks had acknowledged that Torrence had allowed her to move into the house and live there.The court said this was important because her stay had begun with Torrence's permission. Her presence in the property did not establish that she had occupied it against Mack's ownership rights.It also found no evidence that the original joint ownership arrangement between Mack and Torrence had ever been ended. Nor could Hicks show that she had taken exclusive control of the house in a manner that would support her ownership claim.The fact that Mack had moved out did not automatically take away her rights over the property. Since she and Torrence had continued to own the house jointly, his death meant that his share passed to her.This left Mack as the sole owner, despite having moved out decades before Hicks began living there.Court rejects demand for money spent on houseApart from seeking ownership, Hicks wanted Mack to repay money she said she had spent on the property. Her claims included contributions towards the mortgage, repairs and improvements, as well as other household expenses.The lower court, however, found that Hicks had not established that Mack had unfairly benefited from her spending. The appeals court agreed that there was no reason to overturn this finding.The earlier judgment noted that Torrence had also used his earnings and Social Security disability benefits to make some mortgage payments. Hicks had contributed towards the loan as well, but her payments were not consistent throughout the period.The court also considered the fact that Hicks had lived in the house for several years. It found that she had received value from the money she spent because she had been able to use the property as her home during that time.Her demand for compensation for mortgage payments and improvements was therefore rejected.Appeals court upholds earlier rulingHicks challenged the lower court's decision on several grounds, including her claim that she had not been given a proper opportunity to question Mack during the trial.However, the appeals court found that Hicks had not taken the required steps to bring Mack into the proceedings as a witness. She had neither included her in the list of witnesses nor taken steps to secure her appearance.The court also noted that Hicks had not raised an objection during the trial. It therefore rejected her argument that she had been denied an opportunity to question Mack.The appeals court further found that Hicks had not provided enough material to show that the lower court had made an error while deciding the case.It ultimately upheld the earlier judgment, confirming Mack's ownership of the Phoenix house and rejecting Hicks's claims for ownership and compensation.You use AI every day. articles.title: California woman bought a house in 1978 and left it to her partner through a trust; after both died, another woman challenged his son's claim to the property, but the court ruled in his favour
articles.summary: A house purchased in 1978 by a California woman became the centre of an inheritance dispute decades later, after her death and that of her long-term
articles.body: A house purchased in 1978 by a California woman became the centre of an inheritance dispute decades later, after her death and that of her long-term partner. Diane Martinez had lived at the Stanton property with Lester Edmond Compton and named him as the sole beneficiary of her trust. However, the property had never been formally transferred into her trust through a deed. After Martinez died in 2020, a probate court recognised the house as an asset of her trust and transferred ownership to Lester. He died less than two months later, leaving his son, John Compton, to establish that the property belonged to his father's trust. Another woman challenged his claim, but an appeals court upheld his position on November 24, 2026.How the California couple arranged their trustsMartinez purchased the Stanton property in 1978 and subsequently lived there with Compton. More than three decades later, on September 12, 2012, the couple created separate trusts to organise their assets and specify who would receive their property.Under the Diane Marie Martinez Trust, Compton was named as the successor trustee and the sole beneficiary of her estate. The separate Compton Trust named Lester as its trustee, Martinez as his first successor trustee and his son, John, as the second successor trustee.Lester's trust also contained an important provision stating that his worldly possessions were to be held for Martinez and, if she died before him, were to pass to John. Alongside this, Lester signed an assignment transferring all his property, including assets acquired in the future, to his trust.Why the house became part of a legal disputeAlthough Martinez's trust identified the Stanton property, she never executed or recorded a deed formally transferring it into the trust. Consequently, the property remained in her name when she died on March 21, 2020.In June 2020, Compton filed a petition seeking an order confirming that the house should be transferred to him as successor trustee of Martinez's trust. On April 20, 2021, the probate court approved his request, declaring the property transferred to him and vesting both legal and equitable title in his name as successor trustee.Compton died on June 14, 2021, less than two months after obtaining the order. This brought the separate trust he had created with Martinez back into focus, particularly the clause covering property he might acquire after signing the document in 2012.Another woman challenged the son's inheritance claimIn August 2022, John Compton approached the probate court seeking confirmation that his father's trust was valid, that he was its sole beneficiary and that the Stanton property belonged to the trust. He also sought authority to manage and control the property as its trustee.Cindy Lynn Cavanaugh objected to the petition in September 2023, arguing that the trust assignment did not adequately identify the house. She relied on California's statute of frauds, which sets requirements for written evidence establishing trusts involving real estate.Her argument was that Lester had not owned the Stanton property when he created his trust in 2012 and that a general assignment covering future property was insufficient to establish ownership of a specific house. The probate court rejected the objection after considering the trust documents, agreed facts, John's testimony and excerpts from Cavanaugh's deposition. It ruled that the property was an asset of Lester's trust, prompting Cavanaugh to appeal.Why the appeals court ruled in the son's favourThe California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division Three, examined whether Lester's signed assignment could cover a property he acquired years after creating his trust.The judges found that the document explicitly covered all his property, regardless of its type, location or when it was acquired. They also relied on the April 20, 2021 probate order, which had formally established that Lester owned the Stanton property as successor trustee of Martinez's trust.The court referred to an earlier California decision, Ukkestad v. RBS Asset Finance, Inc., which recognised that real estate can become part of a trust without a separate deed when the required written documentation and evidence identify the property.Applying that reasoning, the judges concluded that Lester's signed assignment, combined with the earlier probate order, was sufficient to establish that the Stanton house belonged to his trust. The court rejected Cavanaugh's arguments and affirmed the lower court's judgment on November 24, 2026.What the ruling means for the propertyThe appellate judgment leaves John Compton's claim to the Stanton property intact. As the sole beneficiary and successor trustee of his father's trust, he can manage and control the property as an asset of that trust.The court also ordered Cavanaugh to pay the respondent's costs of the appeal. However, the judgment did not specify the property's market value or award a separate monetary payment.The ruling also does not establish that Cavanaugh lived in the house or identify her relationship to Martinez or Compton. Its central finding concerns the validity of Lester's assignment of future-acquired property and whether the Stanton house consequently became part of his trust.You use AI every day.
