articles.title: The black & white of why South Africa took unique step to destroy its nuclear weapons
articles.summary: Last week, the leaders of the United States, Russia and China held a trilateral in Shenzhen and came to a common conclusion: Nuclear war \"cannot be won
articles.body: Last week, the leaders of the United States, Russia and China held a trilateral in Shenzhen and came to a common conclusion: Nuclear war "cannot be won and must never be fought".The big three also agreed to hold a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons. However, none of them announced specific commitments to reduce their arsenals.Turns out, the only country known to have independently developed nuclear weapons and subsequently dismantled its entire arsenal is South Africa.However, the decision wasn’t taken as a step to pursue global peace objectives.The denuclearisation came just before the country's transition from white-minority rule to a black-majority-led democratic government, raising significant debates about the intent and reasons that led to the decision.Did the apartheid government dismantle its nuclear weapons because it did not want an incoming African National Congress (ANC)-led government to inherit them? Or had changing geopolitical circumstances made the arsenal unnecessary? The answer involves a combination of political, security and diplomatic considerations, with the precise weight of each factor still debated.Nucleus of South African politicsApartheid was a system of institutionalised racial segregation and white-minority rule in South Africa. It became official government policy after the National Party came to power in 1948.Under the system, the Black majority was denied meaningful political representation and subjected to racial discrimination in housing, education, employment, land ownership and access to public facilities. The government maintained white political control through discriminatory laws, restrictions on movement, forced removals and state repression.The African National Congress (ANC) emerged as the principal organisation opposing the system. Its leaders included Nelson Mandela, who spent 27 years in prison for his involvement in the anti-apartheid struggle.The political transition began under President F.W. de Klerk, who took office in September 1989. On February 2, 1990, he announced that the ANC and other banned organisations would be legalised. Mandela was released from prison nine days later.Negotiations between the government and anti-apartheid organisations eventually paved the way for South Africa's first democratic elections on April 27, 1994. The ANC won the election, and Mandela became the country's first Black president.But before the transfer of political power, the apartheid government had already taken a significant decision concerning South Africa's nuclear capabilities.A nuclear deterrentSouth Africa's nuclear weapons programme emerged during the Cold War, when the apartheid government feared the expansion of Soviet and communist influence in southern Africa.The independence of Angola and Mozambique in 1975, the civil war in Angola and the presence of Cuban troops in the region reinforced Pretoria's security concerns. The government also feared that its growing international isolation could leave it without external military support in the event of a conflict.In 1974, the government approved development of a limited nuclear deterrent. The programme eventually produced six completed nuclear devices, while a seventh remained under construction when the decision to terminate it was taken in November 1989.The weapons were relatively simple gun-assembled fission devices, rather than sophisticated thermonuclear weapons. Their intended role, according to de Klerk's subsequent account, was primarily deterrence.The strategy was also unusual. Rather than planning to use the weapons in a conventional nuclear exchange, the government envisaged revealing its capability to a major power, such as the United States, in a severe regional crisis in the hope of prompting outside intervention.In a speech to Parliament on March 24, 1993, de Klerk said the programme had been initiated in response to the perceived Soviet threat and the build-up of Cuban forces in Angola.Why did South Africa dismantle its nuclear weapons?De Klerk took the decision to terminate the programme in November 1989, shortly after becoming president. On February 26, 1990, he issued a written instruction directing that all existing nuclear devices be dismantled and the nuclear material returned to the Atomic Energy Corporation (AEC).The timing is significant. The order came after the ANC had been unbanned and Mandela released, but more than four years before the first democratic elections.The possibility that an incoming ANC-led government could inherit nuclear weapons has consequently remained one of the most debated explanations for the decision.Waldo Stumpf, former head of South Africa's Atomic Energy Corporation, later recalled that de Klerk believed transferring nuclear weapons to an incoming government would complicate the handover of power because they would become a "hot potato".A 2025 study by historian Robin E. Möser examined the political and diplomatic calculations behind South Africa's disarmament using archival material and interviews with former officials.The study noted that the possibility of a future ANC government inheriting the arsenal had concerned international observers. However, it found little in the South African archival records to establish that this was a decisive consideration for de Klerk and his advisers.The study suggested that dismantling the arsenal also served the outgoing National Party government's domestic political interests. By giving up nuclear weapons and embracing non-proliferation, the government could secure international goodwill and support for its political reform process before negotiations and democratic elections determined the country's future.The concern about transferring the weapons therefore cannot be dismissed, but neither can it be established as the principal reason.End of the Cold War and changing security environmentAnother major explanation was the transformation of South Africa's regional and international security environment.The withdrawal of Cuban troops from Angola, Namibia's independence in 1990 and the weakening of Soviet influence reduced the perceived military threat that had helped justify the nuclear programme.De Klerk himself cited these developments in his March 1993 parliamentary address. He argued that the Cold War had effectively ended and that South Africa had an opportunity to move away from confrontation towards cooperation with its neighbours and the international community.Dr Rashmi Rani Anand, assistant professor at the Centre for African Studies, School of International Studies, Jawaharlal Nehru University, described the decision as involving both domestic political considerations and international non-proliferation pressures."The dismantling of South Africa's nuclear arsenal is a multifaceted issue involving both domestic transition concerns and international non-proliferation pressures," she said.Addressing the possibility of the ANC inheriting the weapons, Anand said: "The possibility of an ANC-led government inheriting nuclear weapons may have influenced the outgoing leadership's calculations. However, one should be cautious about presenting this as the principal reason for South Africa's nuclear disarmament."She added that "an equally important strategic explanation lies in the transformation of its regional and global security environment"."The end of the Cold War and the weakening of the Soviet Union significantly reduced the perceived communist threat," Anand said.Dr Ashok Sharma, visiting fellow at the University of New South Wales Canberra at the Australian Defence Force Academy, similarly emphasised that multiple considerations shaped the decision."South Africa's nuclear disarmament was driven by a combination of strategic, domestic political and international considerations," he said.Sharma added: "The end of the Cold War, Cuban military withdrawal from Angola and Namibia's independence substantially diminished South Africa's perceived external security threats."International rehabilitation and the NPTSouth Africa's international isolation was another important factor.The apartheid system had attracted international condemnation, sanctions and an arms embargo. Its secret nuclear weapons programme further complicated relations with other countries and limited access to international nuclear cooperation.De Klerk argued that abandoning the arsenal would help normalise South Africa's international relations and allow it to participate more fully in international nuclear technology exchanges.South Africa acceded to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) on July 10, 1991, as a non-nuclear-weapon state. It subsequently signed a comprehensive safeguards agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) on September 16, 1991, placing its declared nuclear materials and facilities under international inspection.Anand said that when de Klerk assumed office in 1989, "nuclear weapons were increasingly seen as an obstacle to South Africa's international rehabilitation, access to civilian nuclear technology and improved relations with African neighbours"."The dismantling of apartheid, nuclear disarmament and accession to the NPT collectively facilitated South Africa's reintegration into the international community and renewed access to global trade, investment and technological cooperation," she said.Sharma also highlighted the importance of the international non-proliferation framework, saying that South Africa's accession to the NPT in 1991 "facilitated its international rehabilitation and reintegration".He argued that the decision should be understood "as a convergence of changing threat perceptions, domestic political transition and international non-proliferation pressures, rather than exclusively as an attempt to deny nuclear weapons to the incoming Black-majority government".Burning the bridgeSouth Africa's denuclearisation involved considerably more than dismantling its six completed weapons.The government also dealt with the incomplete seventh device, recovered the highly enriched uranium (HEU) from the weapons and took steps to eliminate sensitive weapons-related equipment and documentation.According to an IAEA report submitted in September 1993, all the HEU had been removed from the weapons, melted down and returned from the Armscor weapons facilities to the AEC by September 6, 1991.The dismantlement procedures also included destroying sensitive weapons components and design information. By March 23, 1993, most classified documents had been destroyed and sensitive weapons components had either been destroyed or damaged beyond reuse.The destruction of documents was particularly significant because it made it harder for any future government to reconstruct the technical details of the weapons programme.However, dismantling the weapons did not mean that South Africa eliminated every stock of highly enriched uranium or all its civilian nuclear capabilities.Anand clarified that the nuclear material was not entirely converted into lower-enriched uranium."To the best of my knowledge, the highly enriched uranium recovered from the dismantled nuclear weapons was subsequently placed under international safeguards. However, not all of it was blended down to lower enrichment levels during the dismantlement process," she said."South Africa continued to retain stocks of highly enriched uranium even after its democratic transition."The IAEA began inspections in November 1991. Following de Klerk's public disclosure in March 1993, its verification work expanded to examine the former weapons programme, its nuclear material and the dismantling of associated facilities.The agency subsequently confirmed that the six completed weapons and the incomplete seventh device had been dismantled and that it had found no indication that the declared programme had not been terminated.South Africa's civilian nuclear research and technology capabilities, however, were not eliminated.'Bomb for Africa'The ANC had opposed the apartheid government's nuclear weapons programme, arguing that it had been developed without the consent of the country's Black majority and posed a threat to regional security.But it was also critical of the secrecy surrounding the programme and the manner in which the dismantlement was conducted.The ANC was not consulted before the original decision was taken. Although reports about South Africa's enriched uranium stocks and nuclear facilities had raised suspicions, the full extent of the programme was publicly disclosed only in March 1993.The ANC welcomed de Klerk's announcement but questioned his explanation that the weapons had been developed to deter Soviet expansionism. In a statement reported by The Independent on March 25, 1993, the organisation described that explanation as "disingenuous, perhaps even cynical", arguing that the weapons were intended to protect the apartheid system rather than deter an external threat.Mandela, meanwhile, supported nuclear non-proliferation and an African nuclear-weapon-free zone. The ANC's broader policy under his leadership was to maintain South Africa's commitment to the NPT rather than revive the arsenal.However, opinions within the liberation movement were not entirely uniform.A few ANC figures reportedly regretted the dismantlement. They included Joe Modise, a senior ANC leader and commander of its armed wing, Umkhonto we Sizwe, who later became defence minister under Mandela.Modise was among those who saw nuclear weapons as a potential source of African strategic influence. "We wanted a bomb for Africa," he is reported to have said.The Mandela government did not reverse the decision. South Africa continued to support the NPT and subsequently backed the Treaty of Pelindaba, which established an African nuclear-weapon-free zone.The gray zoneSouth Africa's nuclear disarmament remains an exceptional case in the history of nuclear proliferation. The apartheid government dismantled its arsenal while still in power, before the ANC could take control of the state.The possibility of preventing an incoming Black-majority government from inheriting the weapons remains a legitimate historical question. Stumpf's recollection and the concerns expressed by foreign officials suggest that the issue was part of the political calculations surrounding the transition.But the available evidence does not establish racial distrust as the principal motivation. The end of the Cold War, the decline of regional security threats, the pursuit of international rehabilitation and the political management of the transition all offer important explanations.South Africa's experience was therefore not simply a story of a country giving up nuclear weapons. It was also a case of an outgoing minority government seeking to shape the strategic and diplomatic inheritance of a country on the verge of democratic transformation.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Whether Yogi ji or someone else': Keshav Prasad Maurya says BJP's CM face will be decided after UP assembly polls
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh deputy chief minister Keshav Prasad Maurya on Wednesday said that the Bharatiya Janata Party's chief ministerial candidate will
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh deputy chief minister Keshav Prasad Maurya on Wednesday said that the Bharatiya Janata Party's chief ministerial candidate will be decided by the elected MLAs after the assembly polls.Maurya said that BJP contests elections on the "lotus flower" and chief ministers are decided after elaborate deliberations."BJP's face at the time of elections is the lotus flower, and elections are contested based on the lotus flower. After the elections, when MLAs are elected, their meeting is held, and central observers arrive," news agency ANI quoted Maurya as saying."Based on that meeting, whoever is decided unanimously then leads. At present, our Chief Minister is Yogi Adityanath ji. Whether Yogi ji or someone else will be chief minister in the future, I cannot decide. The MLAs elected at that time will decide it," he added.Asked directly whether he supports Yogi Adityanath, Maurya replied, "Yes, I do."When asked if he could himself be a contender, he said, "No individual decides this. SP, BSP, and Congress are private limited companies.""We have a system here. Whenever the leader of the legislative party is chosen, central observers come after the election. articles.title: Russian missile enters Poland, Gripen fails to intercept: How bad weather disrupts fighter jet operations
articles.summary: A Russian cruise missile entered Polish airspace, prompting a Swedish Saab Gripen fighter jet to move in for an interception.
articles.body: A Russian cruise missile entered Polish airspace, prompting a Swedish Saab Gripen fighter jet to move in for an interception.But despite approaching the incoming threat, the fighter was unable to shoot it down as bad weather prevented the pilot from positively identifying the target.The incident highlights how adverse weather conditions can complicate even advanced fighter jet operations, affecting their ability to detect, track and engage enemy threats.The incident took place on November 20, amid a major Russian aerial attack on Ukraine. According to reports, Russian cruise missiles entered Polish airspace, prompting Nato to scramble fighter jets to monitor and respond to the potential threat.Two Swedish Gripen fighters joined Polish F-16s in the air-defence operation. One of the Swedish pilots approached an object believed to be a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile and received conditional authorisation to engage it.However, the pilot ultimately withheld fire because poor weather conditions prevented positive identification of the target.Polish military officials later disclosed details of the encounter, highlighting the challenges Nato fighters faced while responding to the Russian aerial threat.How bad weather affects fighter jet operationsBad weather can pose a major challenge to military aviation, affecting everything from target detection and weapons accuracy to flight safety and mission planning.Despite advances in radar, infrared sensors and precision-guided weapons, fighter aircraft are not completely immune to atmospheric conditions.The US Air Force, in its Air Force Doctrine Publication 3-59 on Weather Operations, acknowledges that weather must be factored into the planning, execution and sustainability of military operations, as it can influence the effectiveness of aircraft and weapons systems.Bad weather can affect fighter jet operations at multiple levels, from detecting enemy targets to engaging them. Heavy cloud cover, fog and precipitation can reduce visibility and affect electro-optical and infrared sensors used for target identification.While radar can continue tracking airborne objects in poor visibility, tracking alone may not be enough to establish whether a target is hostile.According to a US military training document on atmospheric effects on electro-optical systems, precipitation and other visibility obstructions can make target acquisition more difficult. Weather can also affect weapons accuracy, particularly laser-guided weapons, which require a clear path to designate targets.US Air Force weather forecaster Sergeant Kaelin has highlighted how certain targeting systems can lose effectiveness when atmospheric conditions reduce the temperature contrast needed for infrared detection.Adverse weather can also threaten flight safety and disrupt combat missions. Thunderstorms, turbulence, lightning, hail and wind shear can make flying hazardous, while ice accumulation can affect an aircraft's aerodynamic performance.The US National Weather Service identifies thunderstorms, turbulence and low-level wind shear as major aviation hazards. Heavy rain, fog, snow and strong crosswinds can also complicate take-offs and landings, potentially delaying fighter launches, aerial refuelling and other military operations. Such disruptions can affect the timing of air-defence responses, particularly when fighters are required to scramble at short notice.Weather can also become a strategic factor in military planning.In an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine, US Air Force Colonel Patrick Williams, director of weather at Air Force Headquarters, explained how militaries can exploit weather conditions to create operational disadvantages for adversaries.Former 557th Weather Wing commander Colonel Bradley Stebbins also cautioned that even carefully planned air operations can fail to achieve their objectives if weather does not permit their execution.The Gripen incident over Poland illustrates this challenge: modern fighter jets may be capable of flying through adverse conditions and tracking potential threats, but their ability to positively identify and engage those targets can still be restricted by the weather.

articles.title: 'Russia wants more than Ukraine': German Chancellor Merz sounds alarm over Moscow's ambitions across Europe
articles.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday issued a stark warning over Russia's ambitions, saying Moscow wants more than just Ukraine.
articles.body: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday issued a stark warning over Russia's ambitions, saying Moscow wants more than just Ukraine.He accused Russia of escalating tensions across Europe, including in the Baltic region, Poland and the Black Sea. Merz also called on European nations to set clear boundaries for Moscow, warning that the threat extends beyond Ukraine's battlefield.Addressing the Bundestag during a debate on Germany's 2027 federal budget, Merz said Russia's actions were not limited to the war in Ukraine and pointed to growing tensions across multiple regions. He also warned of Russian escalation in outer space and within Germany's own borders, saying it was taking place "even at the cost of human lives"."Anyone who fails to grasp this either does not understand the world as it is, or is pursuing an entirely different agenda, one that stands in opposition to the freedom, openness, and liberal values of our own country," Merz said.He asserted that Europe must respond firmly to Moscow's actions, adding, "We, as Europeans, must and will set clear boundaries for Russia."Merz's warning came as he made a broader case for strengthening Germany's security and addressing long-standing domestic challenges.He said the country had neglected fundamental issues for too long, particularly defence, infrastructure, demographic change and the economy, and stressed the need to address them urgently.On defence, Merz argued that Germany could no longer afford to overlook the changing security environment in Europe. He linked the need for stronger military capabilities to Russia's growing assertiveness and called for a more decisive European response to protect the continent's security.The warning also comes against the backdrop of Germany's changing defence policy following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Berlin has since moved to increase military spending, strengthen its armed forces and reduce its dependence on Russian energy, marking a major shift from its earlier approach towards Moscow.You use AI every day. articles.title: Christian filmmaker's discovery of Jewish roots sparks mission to uncover centuries-old secret
articles.summary: Evangelical Christian Laurie Cardoza-Moore says her film traces Anussim, descendants of Jews forced to convert during the Inquisition around 500 years ago.
articles.body: A leading evangelical Christian leader has embarked on a journey to trace the descendants of Jews forcibly converted to Catholicism in Spain and Portugal during the Inquisition around 500 years ago, hoping to help those of Hispanic and Latino descent, known as Anussim or crypto-Jews, rediscover their Jewish roots. Through her film, "The Lost Jews of the Inquisition," Laurie Cardoza-Moore told Fox News Digital that she hopes to help people like herself uncover a history they may not even know their families carry. She says the Israeli government believes there could be millions of "Anussim," or hidden Jews. "Some know their family history, while others don’t," she said. CHRISTIAN LEADERS HOLD EMERGENCY SUMMIT IN JERUSALEM TO CONFRONT GLOBAL RISE IN ANTISEMITISM Emmy Award-winning documentary filmmaker and host of the television show "Focus on Israel," Cardoza-Moore also serves as president of Proclaiming Justice to the Nations (PJTN). She is also a member of the Tennessee Textbook and Instructional Materials Quality Commission. For Cardoza-Moore, the journey began in 2002, in the aftermath of 9/11, when she decided to introduce a resolution in the Tennessee state legislature expressing support for Israel in its war on terror. The following year, she was invited by the Jewish Federation of Nashville on a mission to Israel. During a visit to the Diaspora Museum at Tel Aviv University, now known as the ANU Museum of the Jewish People, Cardoza-Moore discovered that the surnames on both her mother’s and father’s sides of the family were of Jewish origin. One Sabbath, the group was hosted by a family from Nashville that had immigrated to Israel. As the family recited the blessing over the challah, in keeping with Jewish tradition, Cardoza-Moore recalled her grandfather making the same bread. She remembered eating it on Friday nights as a child, when she called it "sweet bread." Cardoza-Moore said memories suddenly began flooding back, including a conversation she had with her grandmother when she was four or five years old. She recalled admiring an anniversary ring her grandfather had bought her grandmother. EVANGELICAL LEADER SLAMS PALESTINIAN OFFICIAL’S BIBLE CLAIMS AS ‘CONTEMPTIBLE’ "I remember saying, ‘Nana, that ring looks fit for a princess,’ and she said, ‘Well, you know we have a Jewish princess in our family,’" she told Fox News Digital. After gathering evidence during the 2003 trip, Cardoza-Moore asked her father to contact her great-aunt to confirm the family's Jewish roots. She learned that her ancestors were Portuguese Jews who had been forced to convert to Christianity hundreds of years earlier. "It was a tradition to conceal the identity of our family’s ancestors, and it was the responsibility of the patriarch or matriarch, whichever lived the longest, to reveal it to the next generation on their deathbed," she told Fox News Digital. "As a student of the Bible, I knew that one day Israel would be restored, that Hashem would bring all 12 tribes back to the land to inhabit the land of their forefathers. I knew this prophetic history would unfold, but discovering that my family was part of this group of people transformed my life," she said. Through her documentary, Cardoza-Moore said she hopes to spread this message beyond Spain and Portugal to the farthest reaches of the world where the Anussim fled, including Brazil, Argentina and Mexico. She continues to travel across Southern Europe and South America to film interviews for the documentary, which is scheduled to premiere in Israel by fall 2027. Cardoza-Moore said the return of the Anussim is particularly significant amid a sharp rise in antisemitism. Yet, 500 years after the Inquisition, some still fear revealing their Jewish ancestry, she said. "This is a disturbing trend. There are groups within Israel working to bridge the gap and help the Anussim return to the land of Israel. That is the purpose of this documentary: to reach those who don’t know their ancestry, as well as those who know but keep it hidden, and help them understand that it is safe to come back and that Israel is waiting for them," she said. Cardoza-Moore recalled speaking at a convention with a woman who approached her with her family and young children. After introducing herself and learning the woman's last name, Cardoza-Moore asked if she was Jewish. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER "She said they were Catholic, and I told her that her last name was Sephardic. Her face lit up. She was excited by the possibility that she might be descended from the Anussim and said she planned to look into her family history," Cardoza-Moore said. Cardoza-Moore said certain surnames, including Nunez and Lopez, can offer clues to Sephardic Jewish ancestry. She explained that in Spain, the "Z" in some surnames was originally an "S," but that Jews who fled to Portugal changed it to a "Z" as a sign of their Jewish identity, allowing them to recognize one another. "There are so many Hispanic and Latino surnames. In fact, one of the people I’m investigating is a country’s leader. I believe he may also be a descendant of the Anussim," she said. "This is a very exciting journey, one that I get to share with others as they begin to realize that this is their family’s story, too. They start recalling things like, ‘I remember when family members would die, we would cover mirrors during the mourning period,’" she said. Another reason Cardoza-Moore decided to produce the documentary was to educate Christians about the Inquisition and the Catholic Church’s treatment of Jews during that period. DOMINICAN REPUBLIC JOINS GLOBAL FIGHT AGAINST ANTISEMITISM WITH LANDMARK MOVE "There are many Christians, particularly evangelical Christians, who would be equally appalled by what was done to the Jewish people in the name of their God. As they learn what was done to the Jews in the name of Jesus, they will wake up and realize that this is unacceptable," she said. Cardoza-Moore said she sees a growing movement among Christians turning away from Israel and the Jewish people, which she attributes to a lack of biblical education. "We at PJTN have to change that. That is why we use the Bible and the Scriptures and refer to the prophets to remind Christians of their teachings, because Christians believe the prophets spoke the truth," she said. As an evangelical leader, Cardoza-Moore said she had considered keeping her Jewish roots private but ultimately decided that fulfilling her calling was more important. "If my ancestors were persecuted and forced into silence because of who they were, that is unacceptable. I will go to my grave fighting insidious hatred and holding the church and Christians accountable, because we are seeing antisemitism rise again and hearing the same blood libels from Christians that were spread in the past," she told Fox News Digital. Genesis 12:3 says, ‘I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you, I will curse; and all peoples on earth will be blessed through you,’" she added.

articles.title: US-Venezuela security pact is a massive blow to China’s grip in the Americas
articles.summary: Beijing is losing its foothold in infrastructure, oil interests, minerals, debt and military presence — and its primary geopolitical ally — in the United States’ own backyard.
articles.body:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s visit to Venezuela dealt a massive blow to China. It was not merely the signing of a military agreement. Rather, the U.S. has reactivated its presence and power in Venezuela, shattering the strategy that China had spent 20 years attempting to establish.

Beijing is losing its foothold in infrastructure, oil interests, minerals, debt and military presence — and its primary geopolitical ally — in the United States’ own backyard.

President Trump is establishing the most significant legacy of his presidency within the Americas by putting an end to the 27-year-old narco-regime . While a reconfiguration of Congress and the Senate lies ahead, their main goal will be aimed at bringing transparency to the legal framework governing the relationship with Venezuela. It is inconceivable that any legislator would cede the military, economic and geopolitical ground secured in Venezuela to China, Russia or Iran ; the political cost would simply be too high and too risky.

Hegseth is the first — and only — U.S. secretary of Defense to set foot in Venezuela in the 21st century. Yet, this was more than just a visit; it was the culmination of Operation Absolute Resolve , which brought Nicolás Maduro to justice on Jan. 3 . The U.S.-Venezuela resolution secured an agreement providing military access, intelligence sharing and training cooperation — and, most importantly, the exclusion of Beijing and other extra-regional powers.

The 2025 National Security Strategy was clear: “After years of neglect, the United States will reassert and enforce the Monroe Doctrine to restore American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere, and to protect our homeland and our access to key geographies throughout the region.” The document also states that America’s “‘Trump Corollary’ to the Monroe Doctrine” will “deny non-Hemispheric competitors the ability to position forces or other threatening capabilities, or to own or control strategically vital assets, in our Hemisphere.”

On Jan. 3, the myths about the strength of Russia’s air defense systems and China’s radars crumbled . The military and operational superiority of the United States was clear against a system that neither heard, nor saw, much less repelled the attack.

After Operation Absolute Resolve, Venezuela’s transformation continues to move forward including key achievements such as the seizure of highly enriched uranium , capture of a Hezbollah terrorist , elimination of the leader of the Tren de Aragua’s gang, the reestablishment of consular relations with Israel and the release of hundreds of political prisoners.

Venezuela’s military realignment with the United States strengthens oversight of Chinese space satellite facilities such as El Sombrero and Luepa — two of Beijing’s 11 space installations in Latin America. China had been expanding its footprint of such spaces throughout the region, but with the arrival of President Trump, this trend began to stall and reverse in Venezuela and other regional nations.

The agreement also opens doors for the long-overdue transformation of the National Armed Forces . Without such a transformation, any changes in Venezuela would remain mere dead letters. The military must advance in its modernization and professionalization, revise its doctrine and implement fundamental principles regarding human and civil rights.

Hegseth said the agreement “reestablishes a renewed military partnership that will allow America to cooperate with the Venezuelan government and Venezuelan military. Training together, partnering together, sharing intelligence.”

Formalizing agreements with the Venezuelan Armed Forces ensures that political accords aimed at democratizing the country are not buried by military or paramilitary forces aligned with Chavismo.

Changes in Venezuela have progressed at an accelerated pace in less than a year. However, political prisoners still await release, democratic elections remain to be held and credible institutions must be rebuilt. Events are taking a historic turn, thanks to U.S. leadership and the desire for freedom among millions of Venezuelans. Peace is being established through strength— not with words, but with concrete action.

Arturo McFields is an exiled journalist, former Nicaraguan ambassador to the Organization of American States, and a former member of the Norwegian Peace Corps. He is an alumnus of the National Defense University’s Security and Defense Seminar and the Harvard Leadership course.

articles.body:
Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia arrived in Spain on Wednesday, ending a long legal and political battle over his status that became a proxy debate for the Trump administration’s immigration agenda.

Abrego Garcia self-deported to Spain, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) confirmed Tuesday , after facing the threat of deportation to an African country. He arrived in Madrid and put up a fist as he entered a van, not speaking to reporters, according to The Associated Press .

The migrant was mistakenly deported last year after President Trump returned to office. The White House acknowledged the error, which became the first major flash point in the administration’s strict crackdown on immigration.

Abrego Garcia was arrested in Baltimore in 2025 and quickly sent to a megaprison in El Salvador, launching a political firestorm. The administration accused him of being part of the gang MS-13, which he and his family have denied.

The Supreme Court ultimately ordered the administration to facilitate his return to the U.S. The president and Salvadoran leader Nayib Bukele both pushed back on the ruling, arguing at the time that it was not in their authority .

In a social media post Wednesday, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said Abrego Garcia covered his own travel costs and made the decision to self-deport after facing an order.

“Kilmar Abrego Garcia departed the United States pursuant to a removal order. He paid for his own flight and received no incentives,” ICE wrote on the social platform X. “He will NEVER be allowed back inside the United States.”

Van Hollen, who visited Abrego Garcia in prison and strongly advocated for his due process rights, said in a statement that he is relieved the Salvadoran man will be safe. The Maryland Democrat, who is running for Senate majority leader next Congress, accused the Trump administration of “persecution.”

“While the Trump Administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation,” Van Hollen said.

“I am relieved that he will be safe, in a country of his choosing, and free — including from this Administration’s constant persecution,” he added.

After Abrego Garcia returned to the U.S., the Justice Department indicted him on charges related to a 2022 traffic stop. A federal judge later tossed the case , accusing the department of being “vindictive.” The administration appealed the ruling.

articles.title: Trump administration rolls out new tariffs on China, EU

articles.body:
The Trump administration on Wednesday proposed new tariffs on more than a dozen countries, including China and the European Union.

The latest levies include 20 percent tariffs on Chinese imports, according to the office of U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The administration also proposed import taxes on goods from the 27 members of the EU, Cambodia, India, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam.

The administration imposed the levies pursuant to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which grants Greer the ability to impose tariffs on countries he determines to discriminate on trade.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” Greer said in a statement.

By issuing the latest tariffs, Greer argued the administration “can level the playing field for Americans and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.”

The administration previously finalized Section 301 duties ranging from 10 percent to 12.5 percent in July, taxing imports from 17 trading partners — including Canada , Mexico and the EU.

Greer’s office imposed Wednesday’s tariffs after it determined the 14 aforementioned countries rely on “certain acts, policies and practices” that are “unreasonable and burden or restrict” U.S. commerce.

The accusations range from alleging the Chinese government supports “state-owned enterprises on non-commercial terms” and fails to protect against forced labor.

The trade representative’s office also accused the EU of promoting production and exports with high volumes of export credit and alleged that India has “inadequate labor protections.”

Greer’s office is still investigating Mexico and Norway, noting Wednesday it has “not made determinations” on those two countries.

The Trump administration has imposed Section 301 levies after the Supreme Court struck down tariffs President Trump unveiled in April 2025 under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).

But small businesses that successfully challenged Trump’s IEEPA tariffs have challenged his Section 301 tariffs, with the U.S. Court of International Trade overseeing the case.

articles.title: Melania Trump says nine children reunited with families amid Russia-Ukraine war
articles.summary: First lady Melania Trump said Wednesday that she has succeeded in reuniting nine children with their families amid Russia’s war against Ukraine. That marks a total of 43 children the first lady has helped return to their families since she became involved in August 2025. Russian President Vladimir Putin is accused of the war crime…
articles.body:
First lady Melania Trump said Wednesday that she has succeeded in reuniting nine children with their families amid Russia’s war against Ukraine.

That marks a total of 43 children the first lady has helped return to their families since she became involved in August 2025. Russian President Vladimir Putin is accused of the war crime of forcibly transferring Ukrainian children to Russia.

Russia has systematically moved an estimated 35,000 Ukrainian children over the course of the nearly five-year, full-scale war, according to the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab (HRL), a nongovernmental organization at the forefront of tracking and identifying stolen Ukrainian children. The group estimates the number of Ukrainian children in Russia is likely much higher.

“As adults, it is our moral imperative to elevate our children above the divisions that power war in order to restore the simple joys of life, immediately,” Trump said in a statement.

“Today, the reunification of nine children with their families occurred with the full cooperation of the Russian and Ukrainian leaders. I remain determined to continue my humanitarian work and bring families together.”

Trump did not provide details of the children’s nationality or circumstances around their separation. The White House, in particular the first lady, has worked to position Washington as a neutral arbiter between Russia and Ukraine to advance diplomacy.

Last month, Trump succeeded in advancing a localized, multiday ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine to evacuate civilians from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine. It was the first successful ceasefire of the war.

Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian Parliament’s commissioner for human rights who helped facilitate the Oleshky ceasefire, said Ukraine has never blocked Russian citizens from leaving the country.

Lubinets said that after Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Russian citizens in Ukraine were allowed to leave the country through land borders.

“After 2022, absolutely easy, went out from Ukraine through Moldova, through Belarus, we never block the Russian children,” Lubinets said in a briefing at the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington, D.C., earlier this month.

“So I don’t know why the White House uses this category like Russian, Ukrainian children. From our side, we appreciate that Melania Trump assisted returning back several groups of Ukrainian children from Russian territory, and she did it and continues doing it from 2025.”

In addition to Trump’s efforts, the Ukrainian organization Save Ukraine has helped rescue 1,945 children from Russia and the Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine.

Ukrainian children taken by Russian forces and officials are moved through at least 210 reeducation and militarization camps, according to Yale University researchers. More than 2,400 Ukrainian children have been systematically relocated to at least 13 facilities in Belarus, according to HRL’s 2023 report.

Hundreds of Ukrainian children have also been illegally placed for adoption in Russia’s adoption system or with Russian families. HRL identified at least one case where a Ukrainian child was reissued a Russian birth certificate, changing their name and place of birth and making it more difficult for nongovernmental organizations and government officials to track Ukrainian children.

The group has also found that two of Russia’s state-owned oil and gas companies, Gazprom and Rosneft, have helped fund and facilitate the transportation and reeducation of Ukrainian children.

“The kidnapping and indoctrination, including military training, of children from Ukraine was ordered by Russia’s President Vladimir Putin and executed by Russia’s federal, regional, and occupation officials,” the HRL wrote in a fact sheet released last week.

“Russia’s security services and criminal investigative agency systematically targeted vulnerable groups of children and transported them to Russia, where regional officials subjected them to re-education and listed children for adoption.”

articles.title: Teesside residents react to energy price increase
articles.summary: People on Teesside share their views on the news energy bills are expected to increase by 26%.
articles.body:
A hike in energy costs in the new year has prompted concerns many families will see a hard winter.

Energy bills are expected to increase by 26% from January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war, with the government saying it will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity.

However, residents in Stockton-on-Tees and Darlington said that was not enough to mitigate the rise of about £440 annually.

Kathleen Simms, from Stockton, said: "If I can't have the heating on, I'm going to end up in hospital."

Simms, who is in remission from cancer and has a lung condition, said: "It's hard to live now, if they put the bills any higher, we don't know what we can live on.

"We rely on food banks and stuff which we don't really like doing, but if it comes to that crunch, we have to."

In Darlington town centre, Alice Smith Burns said she was fortunate she could "suck up" the extra charges as she lived with her parents, but knew that option was not available to everyone.

"I have my daughter with me, and I'd rather she's not just sat there with blanket on her," Smith Burns said. "I'd rather she just had that heat source.

"I think especially as a young parent, if there are other young parents out there, it might be harder for those kinds of people.

"For low income households, it's a massive toll on everyone."

Alexandra Blowers said she was fortunate to have solar panels on her home as they had brought her electricity bills down.

However, she still predicts she will limit her heating use.

"The gas price is obviously not the cheapest right now," she said.

"We do tend to not put the heading on as much as we might like to, I layer up because I do tend to get quite cold."

Tim Robinson said he also felt fortunate as he would not be hit by the 26% rise immediately due to being on a fixed rate.

However, he said he did not know how others would cope.

"I think the vulnerable always have to be protected no matter what circumstance they're in, whether it's in relation to heating, energy or food," he said.

"If you don't look after the vulnerable in society, then you're a very poor society."

Staff at Stockton Citizens' Advice said they expected to see a wave of people already in debt accessing services in the coming months.

"We know our clients are struggling enough as it is anyway," said CEO Sarah McPhie.

"We know that in the Tees Valley, 70% of those children who are growing up in poverty are coming from a working household and unfortunately those working households are not going to see the increase in their wages compared to the increase in their energy prices."

If he doesn’t want his military vessels hit,…
articles.body:
Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine’s minister of foreign affairs, told Russian President Vladimir Putin to “stop complaining” about attacks on oil refineries following tit-for-tat strikes between the countries targeting energy facilities.

“If Putin doesn’t like Ukraine’s strikes on his oil refineries, he can order an end to the war. If he doesn’t want his military vessels hit, he can order an end to the war,” Sybiha wrote on social platform X . “Not to mention the 432,000 Russian soldiers he has lost on the battlefield this year without coming any closer to the goals of his invasion.”

“Clearly, he doesn’t care about them. Stop complaining. End the war,” he concluded.

The number of Russian soldiers who died while in active combat cited by Sybiha couldn’t be verified.

President Trump decried Ukrainian strikes targeting Russian oil refineries, urging Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to cease the attacks.

Putin reportedly told his fuel and energy sector commission that Russia would invariably retaliate against Ukraine because of the attacks on its energy facilities even as Trump urged against it, Russian state media agency Tass reported.

“I would like to note that retaliatory action from our side is inevitable. Everyone must be aware of that,” Putin stated, per Tass.

Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy targets marked a flash point between Trump and Zelensky as the pair publicly disagreed on their necessity. The strikes created fuel shortages in Russia and prompted Moscow to retaliate on Ukrainian urban gas stations.

The Trump administration previously threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons sales to Europe for Ukraine if Kyiv didn’t stop its strikes on Russian oil refineries.

“I said, look … our lives are more important than the price of energy,” Zelensky said in September while defending the attacks.

Trump announced an energy ceasefire in October between Russia and Ukraine, with both countries agreeing to not hit the other country’s energy infrastructure.

Zelensky broke the truce a few days later, accusing Russia of first breaking the agreement by attacking Ukrainian energy facilities.

The Ukrainian president has expressed frustration with Trump’s proximity to Putin — particularly Trump’s Russian diesel deal. The agreement allowed a certain amount of Russian diesel to enter the U.S. and global marketplace despite global embargoes against the country.
